strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem: current brain-decoding evaluation metrics saturate and diverge from human judgment, and the paper convincingly demonstrates this discrepancy with a carefully collected human study (1,000 image pairs, 22 raters, MTurk with quality filters).

The proposed SEED metric is well-motivated, interpretable, and composed of complementary components (Object F1 via MM-Grounding-DINO, Cap-Sim via GIT + Sentence Transformer, EffNet correlation), with a thorough meta-evaluation against human ratings using multiple correlation measures (pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson) and comparison against alternative candidates (BLIP, CLIP-FlanT5 VQA scores).

The pairwise hinge loss is validated across three reproduced state-of-the-art models (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain) and four subjects, showing consistent improvements in both existing metrics and SEED, plus qualitative evidence.

Valuable resource contribution: the authors commit to open-sourcing the human evaluation results, and the analysis of 'semantic near-miss' phenomena and worst-case judgments (Fig. 4, Fig. 11, Table 2) provides useful insight into failure modes of both metrics and models.

Comprehensive supplementary material: ablations on Object F1 design choices (size/location/number weighting), component combinations (Table 5), re-evaluation of pretrained models (Table 6), and implementation details/code for the loss.
weaknesses: Circularity/overfitting concern in metric design: the SEED combination (Object F1 + Cap-Sim + EffNet) was selected by examining correlations with the same 1,000 human ratings on which it is subsequently reported as best (Fig. 3, Table 1). There is no held-out validation of the metric combination (e.g., new human ratings on a disjoint set or on reconstructions from a different model), so the reported superiority of SEED may be partly an artifact of selection on the meta-evaluation set.

The human study covers reconstructions from only a single model (MindEye2) on four subjects; whether SEED's alignment with human judgments generalizes to other decoding models' outputs is unverified, limiting the claim that it is a general 'go-to metric'.

Component-level biases are acknowledged but not fully resolved: Object F1 is restricted to 82 COCO categories (missing scene-level semantics, as shown in the worst-case analysis), and Cap-Sim/EffNet inherit biases of GIT, Sentence Transformer, and ImageNet-pretrained encoders; no comparison with stronger perceptual similarity metrics (e.g., LPIPS, DreamSim) or learned meta-metric baselines trained on the human data.

Novelty of the pairwise hinge loss is limited—it is essentially a triplet-style ranking loss on CLIP cosine similarities—and the magnitude of improvement on SEED is modest for some models (e.g., MindEye2: .475 vs .474), with per-model hyperparameter tuning that complicates reproducibility.

The simple unweighted average of three heterogeneous metrics (Eq. 6) is ad hoc; no principled weighting or learned aggregation is explored, and the justification relies on the same post-hoc combination search mentioned above.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: the paper convincingly shows that current two-way identification metrics saturate (near-perfect scores) and correlate poorly with human judgments, which is an important issue for a field claiming near-solved status.

Collection and planned release of 1,000 human-rated GT/reconstruction pairs from 22 evaluators is a genuinely useful community resource and enables proper meta-evaluation of metrics, which most prior decoding work lacks.

The proposed metrics (Object F1 via MM-Grounding-DINO, Cap-Sim via GIT + Sentence Transformer) are interpretable, pool-free, and the threshold-averaging scheme for removing hyperparameter dependence is a thoughtful design choice.

Good analysis sections: worst-case judgment analysis (Fig. 4, Tab. 2), the semantic near-miss quantification (17.5%-20.6%), and metric-combination heatmap (Fig. 3) provide insight beyond just reporting a new number.

The pairwise hinge loss is model-agnostic and validated across three different decoding frameworks (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain) with both reproduced and author-provided checkpoints (Tab. 3, Tab. 6), plus hyperparameter details and code in the supplementary.
Honest limitations section and ablations (Tab. 4, Tab. 5) examining why certain components (size/location/number weighting) were excluded.
weaknesses: The human evaluation data is collected only for reconstructions from a single model (MindEye2 on four subjects). The meta-evaluation claim that SEED aligns best with human judgments may not generalize to reconstructions from other models or future, better models; a metric validated on one model's output distribution is a narrow foundation for a 'go-to metric' claim.

SEED is a simple unweighted average of three metrics, and the specific combination was selected by searching all possible combinations against the same 1,000 human ratings used for the final meta-evaluation (Sec. 6.3, Fig. 3). This risks overfitting the metric to the meta-evaluation set; there is no held-out human data or cross-validation to confirm the combination generalizes.

The absolute agreement numbers are modest: SEED achieves .621 Kendall tau and 81.0% pairwise accuracy, meaning it still disagrees with humans on roughly 1 in 5 pairwise judgments. The improvement over standalone EffNet (.599 Kendall) is incremental, and no statistical significance tests are reported for any meta-evaluation comparison.

Novelty of the individual components is limited: Object F1 is a standard precision/recall over detector outputs, Cap-Sim is caption similarity via existing models (closely related to text-to-image evaluation work like [17]), and the pairwise hinge loss is essentially a standard ranking/triplet-style loss on cosine similarities. The contribution is mostly assembly and application rather than new methodology.

The pairwise hinge loss improvements on existing metrics are inconsistent and sometimes marginal (e.g., MindEye2 PixCorr 268 vs 267, Cap-Sim .541 vs .541; UniBrain SwAV .422 vs .426 worse), and reproductions were performed with a reduced latent dimension (4096 vs 4096 for MindEye2 is stated, but other deviations like dimension 1024 for shared latent space) make direct comparison to published baseline numbers unclear.

Only 5-Likert ratings from paid MTurk workers at $0.03 per pair raise annotation quality/consistency concerns; no inter-annotator agreement statistics, filtering of noisy raters, or analysis of rating reliability are reported.

The metric depends on several external models (MM-Grounding-DINO limited to 82 COCO categories, GIT, Sentence Transformer, EffNet), inheriting their biases; failure cases (Fig. 4, Fig. 11) show each component can fail badly, and averaging three flawed metrics is a heuristic without theoretical justification.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the mismatch between automated metrics and human judgment in visual brain decoding evaluation, supported by a compelling motivating example (Fig. 1) showing near-perfect metric scores despite semantically wrong reconstructions.

Provides a substantial human evaluation resource: 1,000 GT–reconstruction pairs rated by 22 annotators on a 5-Likert scale, with clear collection protocol (MTurk Masters, filtering), and a commitment to release the data — a valuable community contribution.

The meta-evaluation (Table 1) is well designed: pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, and Pearson correlation against human judgments, covering the eight standard metrics plus sensible alternatives (BLIP/CLIP-FlanT5 caption similarity), and reveals that only EffNet correlates well with humans — a genuinely informative finding.

The proposed metric components are interpretable and well-motivated: Object F1 via MM-Grounding-DINO with threshold averaging, Cap-Sim via GIT captions + Sentence Transformer, combined with a correlation-based EffNet. Ablations (Tables 4, 5) justify design choices (e.g., excluding size/location/number weighting) and the metric combination.

Analysis goes beyond aggregate correlations: worst-case judgment analysis (Figs. 4, 11), the ImageNet class-dependence analysis of EffNet (Table 2), and the quantification of the 'semantic near-miss' phenomenon (17.5–20.6% rates) provide useful insight into failure modes of both metrics and decoding models.

The pairwise hinge loss is evaluated across three distinct decoding models (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain) with reproduced baselines, showing consistent improvements on both existing metrics and SEED, with hyperparameter search and implementation details (including code) provided in the supplementary.
Well-written and clearly organized paper; limitations (e.g., no perceptual aspect) are acknowledged honestly.
weaknesses: The meta-evaluation is based on reconstructions from a single decoding model (MindEye2) on a single dataset (NSD). It is unclear that SEED's superior alignment with human judgment generalizes to other decoding models, datasets, or reconstruction quality regimes — a notable limitation for a paper whose central claim is about metric validity.

SEED is a simple unweighted average of three metrics (Eq. 6). The combination choice is justified post-hoc via which combination correlates best on the same human data used for meta-evaluation, raising a risk of overfitting the human ratings; validation on held-out ratings or a second dataset would strengthen the claim.

Potential circularity concern: SEED's components (CLIP-adjacent EffNet, caption similarity) overlap conceptually with the CLIP-embedding alignment objective of the proposed pairwise hinge loss, so improvements on SEED for models trained with L_pair may be partially self-fulfilling. The paper does not analyze this.

Novelty of the pairwise hinge loss is moderate: it is a rank-based variant of existing CLIP distillation losses (soft-CLIP), and the paper itself notes prior work uses distillation losses; the empirical gains, while consistent, are modest on several metrics (e.g., PixCorr/SSIM essentially unchanged, some low-level metrics slightly decrease).

The human ratings capture only 'semantic similarity' of the main idea, while the paper's own worst-case analysis shows nuances (scene context, attributes, counting); the metric-human agreement ceiling (Kendall .621) suggests substantial unexplained disagreement that is not deeply analyzed.

Some claims about two-way identification metrics (incomparability across models due to different pools) are argued but not empirically demonstrated, and the objection that a reconstruction 'only needs to be closer than a random example' is partially addressed in the literature.
SEED's computational cost (three foundation models: MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, Sentence Transformer, plus EffNet) is not discussed, which matters for a proposed 'go-to metric.'

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the community currently relies on saturated two-way identification metrics that may mask real semantic failures of brain decoding models, and the paper provides convincing evidence (Fig. 1, Table 6) that SOTA models with near-perfect identification scores still miss key semantics.

Careful meta-evaluation methodology: 1,000 GT-reconstruction pairs rated by 22 evaluators with high inter-rater agreement (ICC 0.84), pairwise accuracy / Kendall / Pearson meta-metrics, and statistical significance testing (bootstrapped CIs excluding zero) for the improvement over EffNet, the strongest existing metric.
Cross-validation of the claim on a second dataset/decoding model (GOD + Mind-Vis, Table 2), which strengthens the generalization argument beyond a single setting.

Thorough robustness and ablation analyses: substitutions of grounding, captioning, and text-embedding models (Fig. 3), VLM-extracted vs. fixed object categories (Table 3), size/location/number weightings (Table 4), all pairwise metric combinations (Tables 5, Fig. 8), and informative worst-case case studies (Sec. 5.3, Appendix D) including honest failure cases of SEED itself (Fig. 10).

Useful downstream analysis: quantification of the 'semantic near-miss' phenomenon (17.5-20.6% across five models) and 'captured objects but missing details' failure mode, which gives the metric practical diagnostic value beyond a single scalar score.

Release of code and human evaluation data supports reproducibility and future metric development; limitations section is candid about dependence on off-the-shelf models and the semantic (rather than perceptual) focus.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: SEED is essentially an unweighted average of three components (object-presence F1 from an off-the-shelf grounding model, caption embedding cosine similarity, and EffNet correlation). Object F1 is restricted to 82 fixed COCO-style categories, which limits coverage for open-vocabulary natural scenes (NSD contains many categories outside the list), and the composition itself is not learned or optimized against human data.

The main meta-evaluation (Table 1) is based on reconstructions from a single decoding model (MindEye2) on a single dataset; the second setting (Table 2) uses only 50 pairs and 10 student volunteers, so evidence for generalization across the model zoo remains thin.

Absolute alignment with human judgment is still imperfect (pairwise accuracy 81%, Kendall 0.62 on the main setting; notably lower on GOD: 73.7%, 0.477), leaving meaningful headroom that the paper does not analyze in depth.

Comparisons with modern perceptual/semantic similarity metrics are incomplete: the paper compares against the eight legacy decoding metrics and VQAScore variants, but does not evaluate established learned image similarity metrics (e.g., LPIPS, DISTS, DreamSim) or direct VLM-based pairwise similarity prompts, which would strengthen the claim that SEED is the best available proxy for human semantic judgment.

The neuroscience motivation (two-stage visual attention) is loosely connected to the actual design; Cap-Sim and EffNet do not clearly map onto the claimed stages, and the framing reads somewhat post-hoc.

Human study details raise minor concerns: $0.03 per pair via MTurk is very low compensation, and although perceptual similarity was collected, it is largely unused in the main analysis; the relationship between semantic and perceptual ratings could have been analyzed more.

Some analysis choices are ad hoc (e.g., fixed confidence threshold 0.3 for near-miss rate, arbitrary cutoffs Object F1 > 0.7 and F1-SEED > 0.2), and the paper acknowledges but does not resolve sensitivity to these choices.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and under-examined question: whether the standard eight-metric evaluation protocol in visual brain decoding actually reflects human judgment, and the identified issues (pooled-comparison dependence, saturation of two-way identification tasks, lack of human-likeness) are well-articulated.

The paper contributes a crowd-sourced human evaluation dataset (1,000 GT/reconstruction pairs from NSD plus a smaller GOD set) with reasonable inter-rater agreement (ICC 0.84/0.93), and commits to releasing it, which has standalone value for the community.

The meta-evaluation protocol (pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson correlation, following established practice) is appropriate, and the statistical significance of SEED's improvement over EffNet is assessed via bootstrapping with reported confidence intervals.

Robustness checks are provided beyond the main result: generalization to a different dataset/decoding model (Mind-Vis on GOD), substitution of the off-the-shelf components (YOLO-World, BLIP-2, Qwen3-Embedding), VLM-generated vs. fixed category lists, and ablations on size/location/number weighting.

The failure-mode analyses (semantic near-miss rate, object-correct-but-detail-missed cases) and honest worst-case analysis (Figs. 4, 9, 10, 11), including failures of SEED itself, add interpretive depth beyond simply proposing a metric.
weaknesses: Limited generalization of the central claim: the meta-evaluation relies on reconstructions from only one decoding model per dataset (MindEye2 on NSD; Mind-Vis on GOD). Since SEED's human-alignment is only demonstrated against the error distribution of these specific generators, the claim that SEED is a broadly better evaluation protocol for the field is stronger than the evidence supports. Evaluating reconstruction pairs from multiple diverse models would be needed.

Missing obvious baselines: the paper does not compare against standard perceptual/semantic similarity metrics from image quality and image retrieval literature, such as LPIPS, DreamSim, DISTS, or SigLIP/DINOv2-based cosine similarity. Without these comparisons it is difficult to establish that SEED is the best available human-aligned measure rather than merely better than the eight decoding-specific metrics.

The proposed method is largely a straightforward composition of off-the-shelf components (MM-Grounding-DINO + GIT + Sentence Transformer + EffNet) with an unweighted average; the neuroscience motivation (two-stage visual attention) is post-hoc and loosely connected to the actual design. The 'neuroscientific inspiration' framing overstates the technical novelty, and the claim that caption-based image-similarity evaluation 'has not been previously proposed' is questionable given Lin et al. (2024) and related VQA/caption-based evaluation work the authors themselves cite.

The improvement over the best existing baseline is modest (Pairwise Acc. 81.0% vs. EffNet's 78.0%; Kendall .621 vs. .559), and the components (Object F1 75.8%, Cap-Sim 73.8%) individually underperform EffNet, raising the question of whether the field should adopt a heavier, three-model pipeline for a ~3-point pairwise-accuracy gain.

Potential circularity concerns: the metric design (object-presence matching, caption similarity) closely mirrors what the Likert-scale instructions asked annotators to judge ('main idea or meaning'), which may partially explain the high alignment; the metric was also tuned in the same population of images used for the meta-evaluation, and no held-out validation of design choices is reported.

The 82-category object list is COCO-derived and may not cover open-world visual content (e.g., the yacht/traffic-light failure); this dataset-specific design weakens the claim of a general semantic metric, and the reported ~0.4 absolute drop when the fixed 82 categories are replaced (Table 3 sensitivity) further undercuts robustness.

Data collection quality concerns: $0.03 compensation per image pair for two Likert judgments on MTurk raises questions about annotator effort and rating quality, which is particularly relevant for a paper whose central argument rests on the reliability of its human ground truth.

Equal weighting of Object F1, Cap-Sim, and EffNet is not justified beyond exhaustive-combination search on the same evaluation data (Fig. 8), which amounts to selecting hyperparameters on the test set; a learned or validated weighting scheme on held-out data is absent.

The failure-mode analyses (Sec. 5.4) rely on arbitrarily chosen thresholds (0.3 confidence, Object F1 > 0.7, Object F1 − SEED > 0.2) and are not validated against human judgment of the identified failure cases, limiting the evidential weight of these findings.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the paper convincingly argues that standard two-way identification metrics in visual brain decoding are near-saturated and poorly aligned with human judgment, and supports this claim with a carefully designed crowd-sourced human evaluation (1,000 GT/reconstruction pairs, 22 raters, ICC = 0.84 for semantic and 0.79 for perceptual similarity), which is itself a valuable community resource.

The proposed SEED metric is well-motivated, with each component (Object F1, Cap-Sim, EffNet) targeting a distinct aspect of semantics; the meta-evaluation protocol (pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson correlation following Lin et al. 2024) is appropriate and SEED achieves the best alignment (81.0% pairwise acc., .621 Kendall, .813 Pearson) with statistically significant improvement over the strongest baseline (EffNet) via bootstrap CIs.

Robustness analysis is thorough: generalization is demonstrated across a second dataset/model (GOD + Mind-Vis), across choices of off-the-shelf grounding/captioning/embedding models (8 combinations), and across VLM-derived vs. fixed object category lists (Appendix B.2, C.3 ablations on location/size/number weighting are a nice touch).

Beyond proposing a metric, the paper yields concrete scientific findings: the semantic near-miss phenomenon (17.5-20.6% rate across five models) and the 'captured objects but missed details' failure mode (8.3-10.7%), plus quantitative re-evaluation of five recent decoding models showing that traditional metrics mask real weaknesses.

Honest treatment of limitations (reliance on off-the-shelf models, OOD failure cases in D.2, degrading utility as perceptual fidelity becomes the priority), plus open code and released human evaluation data.
weaknesses: The headline improvement over the strongest existing metric (EffNet) is relatively modest: SEED improves pairwise accuracy from 78.0% to 81.0% and Pearson from .748 to .813; EffNet alone already captures most of the human alignment, which somewhat weakens the practical significance of the new composite.

The main meta-evaluation (Table 1) is built on human ratings of a single decoding model's reconstructions (MindEye2 on NSD); the secondary validation (GOD/Mind-Vis) uses only 50 reconstructions and 10 student volunteers, so the breadth of reconstruction quality/style in the human data is limited.

SEED is a simple unweighted average of three heterogeneous metrics (Eq. 7); the equal weighting and the choice of the three components are essentially empirical rather than principled, and the neuroscience 'two-stage visual attention' motivation is somewhat post-hoc relative to the design.

The claim that caption-based image similarity evaluation 'has not been previously proposed' is a bit strong given the extensive caption/VQA-based evaluation literature (VQAScore, image-to-text evaluation); although the authors compare against VQAScore variants, positioning against that literature could be deeper.

Some analyses rely on arbitrary thresholds (e.g., Object F1 > 0.7 and Object F1 - SEED > 0.2 for the detail-miss criterion), and the semantic near-miss rate depends on a fixed 0.3 confidence threshold and the 82-category list, raising concerns about sensitivity of the reported failure-mode statistics.

Because both Cap-Sim and Object F1 depend on pretrained captioning/grounding models, potential systematic biases (e.g., against distorted or OOD reconstructions, as the authors themselves show in D.2) could compound rather than cancel in the composite; robustness across model swaps does not fully rule out shared biases across all tested models.
